lines: There is a particular kind of hour, somewhere between waking and being useful, that I have come to defend like a small, ridiculous country.
It has one law: nothing is allowed to be accomplished.
For years I treated mornings as a launch window.
I rose, I optimised, I answered.
The day arrived pre-packaged with demands, and I marched through them like a person assembling furniture in the dark.
I was efficient, and I was nobody.
Now I make tea in the same chipped cup.
I stand at the window and watch the neighbour's lemon tree do absolutely nothing, magnificently.
I let the first thought arrive and sit down, uninvited, like a cat, before I decide whether I want it on my lap.
It is a kind of tuning.
You cannot play an instrument you have not listened to.
The slow hour is where I find out what key I am in today.
And only then, humming, do I open the door.
